title: Model Optimization Toolkit 🧰
description: Quantization‑aware training, pruning, and clustering to maximize model efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.

slides.title: Beyond Post‑Training Quantization 🚀
slides.content:
# When Post‑Training is Not Enough

Post‑training quantization (dynamic/float16/int8) often works great. But for some models, the accuracy drop is too large.

**Quantization‑Aware Training (QAT)** simulates quantization during training, so the model learns to compensate. It gives much better accuracy after quantization.

> Analogy: Practicing a speech with a slightly muffled microphone so you can still sound clear when the real mic is fuzzy.

slides.title: Quantization‑Aware Training (QAT) in TensorFlow 📚
slides.content:
# How QAT Works

- Inserts fake quantization nodes into the model (quantize → dequantize).
- During forward pass, weights and activations are rounded to lower bit‑width, then restored.
- The model learns to be robust to this rounding error.
- After training, the fake nodes are replaced with true quantized operations.

```python
import tensorflow_model_optimization as tfmot

qat_model = tfmot.quantization.keras.quantize_model(model)
# Then compile and train as usual
```

quizData.question: When is quantization‑aware training most beneficial?

options.text: When the model is already very small
When post‑training quantization causes a significant accuracy drop
When converting to TFLite without quantization

quizData.explanation: QAT recovers accuracy lost due to aggressive quantization by simulating it during training.

slides.title: QAT Example (Conceptual)
slides.content: Use the TensorFlow Model Optimization Toolkit (`pip install tensorflow-model-optimization`).
slides.codeSnippet:
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_model_optimization as tfmot

# Original model
model = tf.keras.applications.MobileNetV2(weights=None, input_shape=(224,224,3), classes=10)

# Apply QAT
quantize_model = tfmot.quantization.keras.quantize_model(model)

# Fine‑tune
quantize_model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
quantize_model.fit(train_ds, epochs=3, validation_data=val_ds)

# Convert to TFLite with int8 support
converter = tf.lite.TFLiteConverter.from_keras_model(quantize_model)
converter.optimizations = [tf.lite.Optimize.DEFAULT]
qat_tflite = converter.convert()

slides.title: Weight Pruning ✂️
slides.content:
# Remove Unnecessary Weights

- Pruning sets the smallest weights to zero during training.
- This creates sparse models that can be compressed (zip‑style) and sometimes run faster with sparse kernels.
- Use `tfmot.sparsity.keras.prune_low_magnitude` to wrap layers.

After pruning, strip the pruning wrappers and convert to TFLite. The sparse model may have lower latency on devices with sparse compute support.

slides.title: Weight Pruning Example
slides.codeSnippet:
import tensorflow_model_optimization as tfmot

pruning_schedule = tfmot.sparsity.keras.PolynomialDecay(
    initial_sparsity=0.0, final_sparsity=0.8, begin_step=0, end_step=1000)
prune_low_magnitude = tfmot.sparsity.keras.prune_low_magnitude

pruned_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    prune_low_magnitude(tf.keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu'),
                        pruning_schedule=pruning_schedule),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')
])
# Compile, train, then strip pruning and convert

slides.title: Weight Clustering 🧬
slides.content:
# Reduce Weight Entropy

- Clustering groups similar weights and replaces them by their centroid.
- Reduces model size via dictionary‑based compression.
- `tfmot.clustering.keras.cluster_weights`.

Often used in combination with quantization. After training, remove clustering and compress.

slides.title: Optimization Order 🧭
slides.content: Apply pruning first, then quantization‑aware training, then clustering. Always fine‑tune after applying each technique.
